newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Nobel fund aims to make millionaires of laureates.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nobel fund aims to make millionaires of laureates.

text.p: Sweden's Nobel Foundation, which manages the money given to Nobel prize winners, has the daunting task of ensuring laureates become instant millionaires as they take home the world's most prestigious awards.
This year prize winners will each receive 7.4 million crowns ($1.12 million), roughly equivalent to the Nobel Prize's value in real terms when the first award of 150,000 crowns was given in 1901.

Fund manager Michael Sohlman said investment strategy had strayed somewhat from Alfred Nobel's will in order to cope with erosion of the endowment, which collapsed in value by two-thirds in its first 50 years.

Nobel, a Swedish scientist, stipulated in his will that most of his estate should be invested in a fund and the income used to reward those who "during the preceding year have conferred the greatest benefit to mankind."

"He wanted all his real assets to be sold and put into safe securities and into gilt-edged bonds, which was reasonable at the time when real interest rates were low or negative," Sohlman said in an interview at the foundation's Stockholm headquarters.
Sohlman, who is the grandson of Ragnar Sohlman who was the original executor of Nobel's will, said the foundation aimed to keep the prize as valuable as it was when it was first awarded.
"Our target now is to keep the prize unchanged in real terms," said Sohlman, who said the fund used a conservative investment strategy.

It was not until 1991 that the fund's value was recovered, thanks to its previous manager Baron Stig Ramel who was one of the few investors to steer clear of the Swedish property crash of the early 1990s.
In that year the foundation raised the value of the award by 50 percent to six million crowns.

Sohlman said the fund, which owns exclusive real estate in central Stockholm and the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo, had the responsibility to ensure the Nobel prizes would exist well beyond the next century.
"We've been in business for 100 years, so 50 years is not on our planning horizon. Our intention is, of course, to go on forever," he said.

"Through diversification we have managed to increase the share of equities but decrease the overall risk. So overall the risk of the portfolio is at the same level as if we had only fixed income," Sohlman said.
The fund posted a profit in 1995 of 176 million crowns before appropriations, down from 221 million crowns in 1994.

Administration costs are high, roughly equal to the amount given away in prize money. This year the foundation will give the Nobel institutions which choose winners 42.2 million crowns for the costs of assessing the candidates.

Nobel week in December each year, where winners and their families are flown to Sweden or Norway to accept their prizes and attend a gala dinner in Stockholm's City Hall or Oslo's Grand Hotel, cost the foundation 5.7 million crowns last year.
Any calculation error would leave the foundation red-faced in front of the world's best mathematicians and economists.
"We had this deplorable situation in 1992 when the laureates were told they were awarded a prize worth $1.2 million and when they came for it they found a prize worth $950,000," Sohlman said.
The fund, which manages capital worth 2.3 billion crowns, realised an 8.3 percent return on assets in 1995.
About 10 percent is invested in Swedish shares, 16 percent in other European shares, 18 percent in U.S. shares, nine percent in Japanese shares and 11 percent in emerging markets.
The fund's heavy exposure to Japanese markets last year, where it had 189 million crowns invested in Japanese funds, capped profits.
"We have changed the geographical weighting, some of which has been successful and some has not. Japan has not produced the result we had expected, but we share this fate with others."
The rest of the fund is invested in equal shares of interest-bearing securities and real estate.
Early critics of the prizes said giving Swedish money away to foreigners was not right, Sohlman said.
But Nobel, who spoke and wrote Swedish, Russian, English, French and German, was emphatic on this point.

"No consideration whatever shall be given to the nationality of the candidates, but that the most worthy shall receive the prize, whether he be a Scandinavian or not," Nobel wrote in his will, dated 1895.

Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, said Swedish institutes should award the literature prize and scientific awards in medicine, physics and chemistry but the peace prize would be awarded in Oslo by members of the Norwegian parliament.
At the time of Nobel's death in 1896, Sweden and Norway were united politically, a union which ended in 1905.
The economics prize was first awarded in 1968 by Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, to commemorate its three hundredth anniversary. ($1=6.5867 crowns)
